stem: What is the main advantage of a distribution-free (nonparametric) test over a parametric one?
correct: Validity does not rest on a distributional family such as the normal.
It stays valid when normality fails.

distractors.text: It always has greater power than the parametric test.
distractors.misconception: ignores that power can be lower when the parametric model holds

distractors.text: It needs no assumptions at all, not even independence.
It uses the actual values of the data more fully than a parametric test.
It works only for categorical data.
It gives estimates with smaller variance in every case.

explanation: Rank tests keep the stated significance level whatever the continuous distribution; the price is a small loss of power when the parametric model is exactly right.

stem: How does the Wilcoxon signed-rank test compare in efficiency with the one-sample $t$ test?
correct: Its efficiency is $3/\pi$ under normality and can exceed 1 for heavy tails.
It loses little power for normal data.

distractors.text: It is always far less efficient than the $t$ test.
distractors.misconception: ignores the high efficiency under normality

distractors.text: It is always more efficient than the $t$ test.
distractors.misconception: ignores that the $t$ test is best under normality

distractors.text: Its efficiency is exactly 1 for every distribution.
It has an efficiency of zero for symmetric data.
Efficiency comparisons are impossible because the tests use different statistics.

explanation: The ARE of the Wilcoxon test relative to the $t$ test never falls below 0.864 for any continuous distribution, which makes it a safe choice.

stem: Let $X_1,\dots,X_n$ be independent with a common continuous cdf $F$. What is the cdf of the sample maximum $X_{(n)}$?
correct: $P(X_{(n)}\le x)=F(x)^n$, since all $n$ observations must be at most $x$.
It is $F(x)$ multiplied by itself $n$ times, one factor per observation.

distractors.text: $P(X_{(n)}\le x)=nF(x)$ for $x$ in the support, with one term for each observation.
distractors.misconception: adds the probabilities instead of multiplying them

distractors.text: $P(X_{(n)}\le x)=1-(1-F(x))^n$, because one observation below $x$ is enough.
distractors.misconception: gives the cdf of the minimum instead

distractors.text: $P(X_{(n)}\le x)=F(x)$, so the maximum has the same law as a single draw.
distractors.misconception: thinks the maximum has the same law as one observation

distractors.text: $P(X_{(n)}\le x)=F(x)^{1/n}$, which rises as the sample size grows.
$P(X_{(n)}\le x)=1-F(x)^n$, the chance that all observations exceed $x$.
distractors.misconception: confuses all below with all above

explanation: The maximum is at most $x$ exactly when each of the $n$ independent observations is, which gives $F(x)^n$. The minimum has cdf $1-(1-F(x))^n$.

stem: For $n$ independent continuous observations, which statement correctly describes $P(X_{(k)}\le x)$, where $F=F(x)$ and $1\le k\le n$?
correct: It is the chance that at least $k$ observations are at most $x$, $\sum_{j=k}^{n}\binom nj F^j(1-F)^{n-j}$.
With $N\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,F)$ the number at most $x$, it equals $P(N\ge k)$.

distractors.text: It is $\binom nk F^k(1-F)^{n-k}$, the probability that exactly $k$ observations lie below $x$.
distractors.misconception: uses exactly $k$ instead of at least $k$

distractors.text: It is $\sum_{j=0}^{k}\binom nj F^j(1-F)^{n-j}$, the probability of at most $k$ observations below $x$.
distractors.misconception: flips the direction of the binomial tail

distractors.text: It is $F^k$, because the $k$ smallest observations must all lie below the point $x$.
distractors.misconception: ignores that the other observations are free and which ones are below

distractors.text: It is $kF(x)/n$, a linear interpolation between the minimum and the maximum of the sample.
distractors.misconception: treats order statistics as proportional to the cdf

distractors.text: It is $F^k(1-F)^{n-k}$, with no binomial coefficient needed for the choice of observations.
distractors.misconception: forgets the number of ways to choose which observations are below

explanation: $X_{(k)}\le x$ exactly when at least $k$ observations are at most $x$, and that count is binomial. For $k=n$ this reduces to $F^n$.

stem: Let $X_1,\dots,X_n$ be iid with a continuous cdf $F$, and let $R_i$ be the rank of $X_i$ in the sample. Which statement is true?
correct: The rank vector is uniform over all $n!$ permutations, whatever $F$ is.
Each assignment of the ranks $1,\dots,n$ to the observations has probability $1/n!$, free of $F$.

distractors.text: The law of the ranks depends on $F$, so rank procedures need $F$ to be known beforehand.
distractors.misconception: thinks ranks carry the shape of the distribution

distractors.text: Each $R_i$ is uniform on $\{1,\dots,n\}$ only when $F$ is symmetric about its centre.
distractors.misconception: believes symmetry is needed for rank laws to be free of $F$

distractors.text: The ranks are independent of each other, because the observations themselves are independent.
distractors.misconception: misses that the ranks always sum to a fixed total

distractors.text: The largest rank is more likely to go to an observation that falls far out in a tail.
distractors.misconception: confuses the size of a value with its rank

distractors.text: The ranks are uniform over the permutations only when the data come from a normal law.
distractors.misconception: ties distribution-free behaviour to the normal law

explanation: Continuity rules out ties and exchangeability makes every ordering equally likely. The ranks are not independent: they always sum to $n(n+1)/2$.

stem: A distribution-free confidence interval for the $p$-quantile $\xi_p$ of a continuous distribution is $(X_{(r)},X_{(s)})$ with $r<s$. How is its coverage found?
correct: It is $P(r\le B\le s-1)$ with $B\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)$, whatever $F$ is.
It is the chance that the binomial count of observations below $\xi_p$ lies in $[r,s-1]$.

distractors.text: It requires $F$ to be normal, since the endpoints are order statistics of the data.
distractors.misconception: thinks order statistics need a parametric model

distractors.text: It is $(s-r)/n$, the fraction of the sample lying between the two endpoints of the interval.
distractors.misconception: confuses coverage of the quantile with the sample fraction

distractors.text: It is $P(B\ge r)$ with $B\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,1/2)$, whatever the value of $p$ is.
distractors.misconception: uses the median probability for every quantile

distractors.text: It tends to 1 as $n$ grows, even when $r$ and $s$ are held fixed.
distractors.misconception: believes more data always raises the coverage of fixed order statistics

distractors.text: It can be made exactly $1-\alpha$ for any chosen level $\alpha$ and any sample size.
distractors.misconception: ignores that the coverage takes only discrete binomial values

explanation: Since $F(\xi_p)=p$, the count of observations below $\xi_p$ is $\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)$, whatever $F$ is. Because the count is discrete, one picks $r,s$ with coverage at least $1-\alpha$.

stem: What does the sign test use in a paired design?
correct: Only the signs of the differences; under the null the count is $\mathrm{Bin}(n,1/2)$.
The number of positive nonzero differences.

distractors.text: The sizes of the differences, ranked from smallest to largest.
The mean of the differences divided by its standard error.
The sum of the squared differences.
The count of differences larger than one standard deviation.
The sign of the sample mean only.

explanation: Zero differences are discarded. The test is for the median of the differences being zero, and needs no symmetry.

stem: How does the Wilcoxon signed-rank test use the differences?
correct: It ranks absolute differences and sums the ranks of the positive ones.
It combines signs with ranks of magnitudes.

distractors.text: It ranks the raw differences from smallest to largest, ignoring signs.
distractors.misconception: ignores the absolute values and signs

distractors.text: It counts only the signs.
It adds the positive differences themselves.
distractors.misconception: uses the values instead of ranks

distractors.text: It compares the group means.
It uses the ranks of the observations from both groups pooled.

explanation: $W^+=\sum_iR_i\mathbf 1\{d_i>0\}$ with $R_i$ the rank of $|d_i|$. It needs the differences to be symmetric about the median under $H_0$.

stem: Under $H_0$, what are the mean and variance of the Wilcoxon signed-rank statistic $W^+$ for $n$ nonzero differences (no ties)?
correct: Mean $n(n+1)/4$ and variance $n(n+1)(2n+1)/24$.

distractors.text: Mean $n/2$ and variance $n/4$.
Mean $n(n+1)/2$ and variance $n(n+1)(2n+1)/6$.
distractors.misconception: gives the moments of the total of ranks

distractors.text: Mean $n(n+1)/4$ and variance $n^2/12$.
Mean $0$ and variance $n$.
distractors.misconception: gives the moments of a normal statistic

distractors.text: Mean $n^2/4$ and variance $n^2/24$.

explanation: Each rank $i$ is included with probability $1/2$, so $EW^+=\tfrac12\sum i=n(n+1)/4$ and $\operatorname{Var}=\tfrac14\sum i^2=n(n+1)(2n+1)/24$.

stem: Which assumption does the Wilcoxon signed-rank test need that the sign test does not?
correct: The differences are symmetric about their median.
Symmetry under the null.

distractors.text: The differences are normally distributed.
The two samples have equal variances.
The observations are independent, which the sign test does not need.
The sample is large.
distractors.misconception: describes an approximation, not an assumption

distractors.text: The data are discrete.

explanation: Without symmetry, a significant signed-rank result may reflect skewness rather than a nonzero median.

stem: What is the treatment of zero differences and ties in the signed-rank test?
correct: Zeros are dropped, ties get average ranks.
Mid-ranks for ties.

distractors.text: Zeros are given the largest rank.
Zeros count as positive differences.
Ties are broken at random in all cases.
Tied observations are always deleted.
Zeros and ties need no special handling.

explanation: With ties, the variance of $W^+$ is reduced by a correction, and exact tables no longer apply.

stem: What does the Mann-Whitney (Wilcoxon rank-sum) test compare?
correct: Two independent samples, through pooled ranks.
Whether $P(X>Y)=1/2$.

distractors.text: Two paired samples through the signs of the differences.
The means of two samples, assuming normality.
The variances of two samples.
Two proportions.
Three or more groups.

explanation: If the two distributions differ only by a shift, the test is a test of equal medians; in general it tests stochastic dominance.

stem: How is the Mann-Whitney statistic $U$ related to the rank sum $W$ of sample 1 (sizes $n_1$ and $n_2$)?

distractors.misconception: confuses with the other sample's statistic

distractors.text: $U_1$ and $U_2$ are independent.

explanation: The smallest rank sum possible is $n_1(n_1+1)/2$, when sample 1 holds the lowest ranks, which gives $U_1=0$.

stem: What are the mean and variance of $U$ under $H_0$ for sample sizes $n_1,n_2$ (no ties)?

distractors.text: Mean $n_1n_2$ and variance $n_1n_2(n_1+n_2)/12$.
Mean $n_1n_2/2$ and variance $n_1n_2/4$.
Mean $(n_1+n_2)/2$ and variance $(n_1+n_2)/12$.
distractors.misconception: uses the total sample size only

distractors.text: Mean $0$ and variance $1$.
Mean $n_1n_2/2$ and variance $n_1n_2(n_1+n_2+1)/6$.

explanation: These give $z=(U-n_1n_2/2)/\sqrt{n_1n_2(n_1+n_2+1)/12}$, with a tie correction to the variance if needed.

stem: What does the quantity $U_1/(n_1n_2)$ estimate?
correct: The chance a random observation of sample 1 beats one of sample 2.
The probabilistic index $P(X>Y)$.

distractors.text: The difference in medians.
The ratio of the two sample means.
The correlation between the two samples.
The significance level of the test.
The probability that the two samples are equal.

explanation: A value of 0.5 means no tendency; values near 1 mean sample 1 almost always exceeds sample 2. It is also the area under the ROC curve.

stem: How are ties handled in the Mann-Whitney test?
correct: Ties get average ranks, and the variance gets a correction.
Mid-ranks are used.

distractors.text: Tied observations are removed from the sample.
Ties are always assigned the lowest rank.
Ties are not possible for continuous data, so they can be ignored in practice.
Ties are broken in favour of the larger sample.
Ties make the test invalid.

explanation: With many ties (such as ordinal ratings), the normal approximation with the tie correction is used instead of exact tables.

stem: What does the Kruskal-Wallis test do?
correct: Whether $k$ independent samples share a distribution, using pooled ranks.
The rank version of one-way ANOVA.

distractors.text: It compares paired measurements with signs.
It tests the equality of $k$ variances.
It tests for a trend over time.
It compares two samples only.
It requires normality in each group.

explanation: A significant result says that at least one group differs; post-hoc pairwise tests (Dunn) show which.

stem: How is the Kruskal-Wallis statistic computed?
correct: $H=\frac{12}{N(N+1)}\sum_i R_i^2/n_i-3(N+1)$, compared with $\chi^2_{k-1}$.
From group rank sums.

distractors.text: $H=\sum_i(\bar R_i-\bar R)$, compared with $\chi^2_{k}$.
distractors.misconception: gives a statistic summing to zero with wrong degrees of freedom

distractors.text: $H=\sum_in_i\bar x_i$, compared with a normal distribution.
From the largest and the smallest group means.
$H$ is compared with $\chi^2_{N-1}$.
distractors.misconception: uses the wrong degrees of freedom

distractors.text: $H$ uses the raw observations, not ranks, and is compared with a $t$ distribution.

explanation: Under $H_0$ every group has expected rank sum $n_i(N+1)/2$, and $H$ measures deviations from it.

stem: What is the Friedman test used for?
correct: Comparing $k$ treatments on the same blocks, ranking within blocks.
A rank analogue of two-way ANOVA.

distractors.text: Comparing $k$ independent groups.
Comparing two independent samples.
Testing for rank correlation between two variables.
Testing whether data follow a distribution.
Estimating a density.

explanation: The statistic $\frac{12}{bk(k+1)}\sum_jR_j^2-3b(k+1)$ uses rank sums $R_j$ across blocks and is approximately $\chi^2_{k-1}$.

stem: How does the Friedman test differ from the Kruskal-Wallis test?
correct: Friedman ranks within blocks; Kruskal-Wallis ranks pooled data.
Related versus independent samples.

distractors.text: Friedman ranks the pooled data across all subjects.
Kruskal-Wallis ranks within blocks.
Both are for independent samples.
Friedman needs normal data.
They give identical statistics.

explanation: A block is a subject measured under every treatment; ranking within it removes subject-to-subject differences.

stem: What are the large-sample null distributions of the Kruskal-Wallis and Friedman statistics?
correct: Both are approximately $\chi^2$ with $k-1$ degrees of freedom.
One fewer than the number of groups.

distractors.text: Both are approximately standard normal.
Chi-square with $N-1$ degrees of freedom.
Chi-square with $k$ degrees of freedom.
An $F$ distribution with $(k-1,N-k)$ degrees of freedom.
Uniform on $[0,1]$.

explanation: For small samples exact permutation tables are used. A significant result calls for pairwise follow-up tests with a multiplicity correction.

stem: What is the Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic for testing $H_0:F=F_0$?
correct: $D_n=\sup_x|F_n(x)-F_0(x)|$, the largest vertical gap.
The maximum gap between empirical and claimed cdfs.

distractors.text: The sum of squared differences between $F_n$ and $F_0$.
The difference between the sample mean and the hypothesised mean.
distractors.misconception: confuses with a test of the mean

distractors.text: The difference of the sample medians.
The area between $F_n$ and $F_0$.
The difference between the largest and smallest observations.

explanation: Compute from the ordered sample: $D_n=\max_i\max\{i/n-F_0(x_{(i)}),\ F_0(x_{(i)})-(i-1)/n\}$.

stem: When is the null distribution of the Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic free of the underlying distribution?
correct: When $F_0$ is continuous and fully specified.
Critical values do not depend on which.

distractors.text: For any $F_0$, including discrete ones.
When the parameters of $F_0$ are estimated from the same data.
Only when the data are normal.
Only for samples of size one.
Never, since it always depends on the distribution.

explanation: If parameters are estimated (the normal with estimated mean and variance), use Lilliefors' modified critical values, which are smaller.

stem: Why is the Anderson-Darling test often more powerful than the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test against tail alternatives?
correct: It weights the tails more heavily.
It stresses tail discrepancies.

distractors.text: It ignores the tails entirely.
It uses only the median.
It is a rank test based on signs.
It does not need a specified distribution.
distractors.misconception: ignores that it tests a null distribution

distractors.text: It uses the largest vertical distance.

explanation: The statistic integrates $(F_n-F_0)^2/\{F_0(1-F_0)\}$, which blows up in the tails and so detects heavy tails. For financial returns tail fit matters.

stem: What does the two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test compare?
correct: Largest gap between two empirical cdfs.
Whether two samples differ.

distractors.text: The means of the two samples.
The variances of the two samples.
The ranks of paired observations.
Only the medians of the two samples.
The sample with the more extreme minimum.

explanation: It is sensitive to differences in location, scale or shape, but most sensitive around the centre of the distributions.

stem: How should a result of a Kolmogorov-Smirnov test with a very large sample be read?
correct: Even a tiny departure can be significant.
The test detects negligible deviations.

distractors.text: A significant result always means the departure is large.
Large samples make the test lose power.
The test is invalid for large samples.
The $p$-value is independent of the sample size.
Nonsignificance proves that $F=F_0$.
distractors.misconception: confuses with proof of the null

explanation: $\sqrt nD_n$ is compared with the Kolmogorov distribution; the 5% point is about 1.36, so $D_n>1.36/\sqrt n$ rejects.

stem: How is Spearman's rank correlation computed?
correct: The Pearson correlation between the ranks.
Rank each variable, then correlate the ranks.

distractors.text: As the Pearson correlation of the raw values.
As the number of concordant pairs minus discordant pairs, divided by the total.
As the correlation between the signs of the values.
As the slope of the regression of ranks on values.
As the average of the ranks of the two variables.
distractors.misconception: gives a mean, not a correlation

explanation: $d_i$ is the difference between the two ranks of observation $i$. $\rho_S=\pm1$ for any strictly monotone relation.

stem: How is Kendall's tau defined?
correct: $(C-D)/\{n(n-1)/2\}$, concordant minus discordant.
Concordance probability minus discordance.

distractors.text: The Pearson correlation of the ranks.
The number of concordant pairs divided by $n$.
The sum of squared rank differences.
$C/D$, the ratio of concordant to discordant pairs.
The largest rank difference.

explanation: A pair $(i,j)$ is concordant if $(x_i-x_j)(y_i-y_j)>0$. Tau has a direct probabilistic meaning, unlike rho.

stem: Which relationship does a rank correlation detect that the Pearson correlation may miss?
correct: A monotone but nonlinear relationship.
Any monotone association.

distractors.text: A relationship that is not monotone, such as a U shape.
A causal relationship.
A linear relationship only.
Independence between the variables.
Only perfect relationships.

explanation: For $y=e^x$ on $x=1,\dots,10$ the rank correlation is exactly 1, while Pearson's is noticeably smaller. Both are near 0 for $y=x^2$ on a symmetric $x$ range.

stem: What happens to Spearman's and Kendall's coefficients if one variable is transformed by a strictly increasing function?
correct: They are unchanged, since the ranks are the same.
Both are invariant to monotone increasing transformations.

distractors.text: They change in proportion to the transformation.
They become exactly 1.
They change sign.
distractors.misconception: is true only for decreasing transformations

distractors.text: They are unchanged only for linear transformations.
They are unchanged only for log transformations.

explanation: A strictly decreasing transformation reverses the ranks and changes the sign of the coefficients. Pearson's correlation is only invariant to linear maps.

stem: Which statement describes the Mann-Kendall statistic $S$ for observations $x_1,\dots,x_n$ recorded in time order?
correct: $S=\sum_{i<j}\mathrm{sgn}(x_j-x_i)$, the number of rising pairs minus falling pairs.
It is Kendall's concordance statistic between the series and its time index.

distractors.text: It sums only the signs of consecutive differences $x_{t+1}-x_t$, ignoring pairs far apart in time.
distractors.misconception: uses adjacent pairs instead of all pairs

distractors.text: It sums the raw differences $x_j-x_i$ over all pairs, so large jumps dominate the value.
It tests only for a straight-line trend and needs normally distributed errors.
distractors.misconception: confuses it with the regression slope test

distractors.text: It equals $n$ times the Spearman correlation between the series and time.
distractors.misconception: mixes up two different rank statistics

distractors.text: It is large only if the series rises in every single period, with no falls at all.
distractors.misconception: demands strict monotonicity period by period

explanation: Every pair $i<j$ contributes $\pm1$ according to the direction of change, so $S$ is the numerator of Kendall's tau between time and the observation. It detects monotone, not just linear, trends.

stem: Under the hypothesis that $n$ observations are iid with no ties, what are the null mean and variance of the Mann-Kendall statistic $S$?
correct: $E[S]=0$ and $\mathrm{Var}(S)=n(n-1)(2n+5)/18$, with $S$ near normal for moderate $n$.
Centred at zero with variance $n(n-1)(2n+5)/18$, so a normal approximation applies.

distractors.text: $E[S]=n(n-1)/4$ and $\mathrm{Var}(S)=n(n-1)(2n+5)/18$, with $S$ near normal for large $n$.
distractors.misconception: takes the mean of the concordant count rather than of $S$

distractors.text: $E[S]=0$ and $\mathrm{Var}(S)=n(n+1)(2n+1)/24$, the same as the signed-rank statistic.
$E[S]=0$ and $\mathrm{Var}(S)=n(n-1)/2$, since there are that many pair signs.
distractors.misconception: treats the pair signs as independent

distractors.text: $E[S]=0$ and $\mathrm{Var}(S)=n(n-1)(2n+5)/72$, as for the number of concordant pairs.
distractors.misconception: uses the variance of the concordant count instead of that of $S$

distractors.text: $E[S]=0$ and $\mathrm{Var}(S)=n(n-1)(n+1)/12$, the same form as the rank-sum variance.
distractors.misconception: borrows the form of the rank-sum variance

explanation: $S=2C-n(n-1)/2$ where $C$ counts concordant pairs, so $\mathrm{Var}(S)=4\mathrm{Var}(C)$. Check $n=3$: $S$ takes values $\pm3,\pm1$ with probabilities $1,2,2,1$ over 6, so the variance is $22/6=3\cdot2\cdot11/18$.

stem: What assumption makes a permutation test valid?
correct: Under $H_0$ the labels are exchangeable.
All relabellings are equally likely.

distractors.text: The data are normally distributed.
The sample is large.
The variances are known.
The observations are paired.
Only the order of the observations matters.

explanation: Exchangeability can fail with unequal variances between groups or dependent data, in which case a plain permutation test can be invalid.

stem: How is an exact permutation p-value computed for a difference in group means?
correct: Enumerate all assignments and find the share at least as extreme.
The share of relabellings with a gap as large as observed.

distractors.text: By comparing the statistic with a normal distribution.
By resampling the data with replacement.
By dividing the observed difference by its estimated standard error.
By counting the sign changes.
By using only the observed assignment.

explanation: With groups of sizes $n_1,n_2$ there are $\binom{n_1+n_2}{n_1}$ assignments; the observed one is included, so the smallest p-value is $1/\binom{n}{n_1}$.

stem: How many distinct assignments exist when $m$ of $N$ units are randomly assigned to treatment?
correct: $\binom Nm$, as order within groups is irrelevant.
Ways to choose the treated units.

distractors.text: $N!$, counting every ordering of the units.
$2^N$, counting all binary labellings.
distractors.misconception: counts labellings that ignore the group sizes

distractors.text: $m!\,(N-m)!$, a product of factorials.
$N\cdot m$, the product of the sizes.
$\binom Nm/2$, halving for symmetry.

explanation: The number of assignments sets the smallest attainable p-value, $1/\binom Nm$, so small experiments can have limited resolution.

stem: What is a Monte Carlo permutation test?
correct: It approximates the permutation distribution with random relabellings.
Random permutations estimate the $p$-value.

distractors.text: It gives exactly the same value as enumeration for any number of draws.
It resamples data with replacement.
It requires a parametric model.
It cannot be used for large samples.
It uses the normal approximation.

explanation: A p-value estimate $(1+\#\{T^*\ge T_{obs}\})/(1+B)$ with $B$ random permutations remains valid.

stem: What is an advantage of permutation tests over $t$ tests?
correct: Exact validity in finite samples under exchangeability.
Any test statistic can be used.

distractors.text: They always have more power.
They need no assumption at all.
They are faster to compute.
They estimate the effect size more accurately.
They work for any dependence structure.

explanation: For the difference in means with many observations, the permutation test is close to the $t$ test, but it also allows medians, trimmed means or ranks.

stem: Let $\hat F_n$ be the empirical cdf of $n$ iid observations from an arbitrary distribution $F$. What does the Glivenko-Cantelli theorem state?
correct: $\sup_x|\hat F_n(x)-F(x)|\to0$ almost surely, for every $F$.
The empirical cdf converges to $F$ uniformly in $x$, with probability one.

distractors.text: $\hat F_n(x)\to F(x)$ at each fixed $x$ but never uniformly over all $x$, however large $n$ is.
The convergence holds only when $F$ is continuous, since jumps in $F$ break the argument.
distractors.misconception: believes jumps in $F$ break the result

distractors.text: The convergence holds only when $F$ has a finite variance, which the proof needs.
$\hat F_n(x)$ equals $F(x)$ exactly once $n$ passes some finite threshold.
$\sqrt n\,\sup_x|\hat F_n(x)-F(x)|\to0$ almost surely, at the same time.

explanation: The theorem holds for every $F$, discrete or continuous, with no moment condition. The supremum is of order $1/\sqrt n$, so after multiplying by $\sqrt n$ it does not vanish.

stem: What is the plug-in estimator of the variance functional $T(F)=\int(x-\mu)^2\,dF(x)$ with $\mu=\int x\,dF(x)$?
correct: $T(\hat F_n)=\frac1n\sum_i(X_i-\bar X)^2$, the variance with divisor $n$.
The mean squared deviation about $\bar X$, from $\hat F_n$ with mass $1/n$ on each point.

distractors.text: $\frac1{n-1}\sum_i(X_i-\bar X)^2$, because plug-in estimators are always unbiased.
distractors.misconception: believes plug-in estimators are unbiased by construction

distractors.text: $\frac1n\sum_i(X_i-\mu)^2$, keeping the true mean $\mu$ inside the sum.
distractors.misconception: plugs in only part of the functional

distractors.text: $\frac1n\sum_i|X_i-\bar X|$, the mean absolute deviation about the sample mean.
distractors.misconception: replaces the functional by a different one

distractors.text: The sample median of the squared observations $X_i^2$, a robust summary of spread.
distractors.misconception: confuses the variance with a median of squares

distractors.text: $\bar X^2$, the square of the plug-in estimator of the mean.
distractors.misconception: confuses the variance with the squared mean

explanation: The plug-in estimator evaluates $T$ at $\hat F_n$. For the variance this has divisor $n$, so it is biased by the factor $(n-1)/n$ but still consistent.

stem: The influence function of a functional $T$ at $x$ is $L_T(x)=\lim_{\varepsilon\to0}\{T((1-\varepsilon)F+\varepsilon\delta_x)-T(F)\}/\varepsilon$. What does it measure?
correct: The effect on $T$ of a tiny contamination at $x$; for the mean it is $x-\mu$, unbounded.
The rate of change of $T$ when mass is added at $x$; for the mean it is linear in $x$.

distractors.text: The effect of deleting the observation $x$ from the sample; for the mean it is $\bar X_{(-x)}$.
distractors.misconception: confuses the influence function with leave-one-out

distractors.text: The density of $F$ at the point $x$, so that for the mean it is simply equal to $f(x)$.
The effect on $T$ of a tiny contamination at $x$; for the mean it is $x-\mu$, a bounded function.
distractors.misconception: believes the mean is a robust functional

distractors.text: The bias of the estimator $T(\hat F_n)$; for the mean it is zero since $\bar X$ is unbiased.
The variance of $T(\hat F_n)$ at sample size $x$; for the mean it is $\sigma^2/x$.
distractors.misconception: confuses influence with the sampling variance

explanation: The influence function is the derivative of $T$ along the path from $F$ towards $\delta_x$. For the mean, $T=\mu$ moves linearly, giving $x-\mu$; the median has a bounded influence function.

stem: Using the influence function $L_T$, the standard error of $T(\hat F_n)$ is approximated by $\hat\tau/\sqrt n$. How is $\hat\tau^2$ computed?
correct: $\hat\tau^2=\frac1n\sum_i\hat L(X_i)^2$, the mean of the squared influence values at the data.
Replace $F$ by $\hat F_n$ in $\int L_T(x)^2\,dF(x)$ and evaluate the integral.

distractors.text: $\hat\tau^2=\frac1n\sum_i\hat L(X_i)$, the average influence value over the sample.
distractors.misconception: forgets to square, although the average is always zero

distractors.text: $\hat\tau^2=\max_i\hat L(X_i)^2$, the largest squared influence value in the sample.
distractors.misconception: uses the largest instead of the average

distractors.text: $\hat\tau^2=\{\frac1n\sum_i\hat L(X_i)\}^2$, the square of the average influence.
$\hat\tau^2=\hat F_n(x)\{1-\hat F_n(x)\}$ for every functional $T$ and every $x$.
distractors.misconception: applies the binomial variance of the empirical cdf to all functionals

distractors.text: It is available only if $F$ belongs to a parametric family, since $L_T$ needs a density.
distractors.misconception: thinks the influence function needs a parametric model

explanation: For the mean $L(x)=x-\mu$, so $\hat\tau^2=\frac1n\sum(X_i-\bar X)^2$ and the standard error is about $\hat\sigma/\sqrt n$, as expected.

stem: Which statement about the Dvoretzky-Kiefer-Wolfowitz (DKW) inequality is true?
correct: $P(\sup_x|\hat F_n-F|>\varepsilon)\le2e^{-2n\varepsilon^2}$ for every $F$ and every $n$.
The band $\hat F_n\pm\sqrt{\log(2/\alpha)/(2n)}$ covers $F$ with probability at least $1-\alpha$.

distractors.text: It holds only asymptotically, and only for a continuous $F$ with a bounded density.
distractors.misconception: thinks the bound is only a large-sample result

distractors.text: The bound is $2e^{-2n\varepsilon}$, so the band shrinks like $1/n$ as the sample grows.
distractors.misconception: misplaces the square and the rate

distractors.text: The bound depends on the density of $F$, so every $F$ needs its own band.
distractors.misconception: believes the band depends on the unknown $F$

distractors.text: The band half-width is of order $1/n$, much narrower than any parametric band.
distractors.misconception: gets the order of the half-width wrong

distractors.text: It controls the error of $\hat F_n(x)$ at one fixed $x$ only, not uniformly in $x$.
distractors.misconception: confuses a uniform bound with a pointwise one

explanation: The half-width is of order $n^{-1/2}$, and the inequality holds for all $n$ and all $F$. To make it at most $\varepsilon$ one needs $n\ge\log(2/\alpha)/(2\varepsilon^2)$.

stem: What is the nonparametric bootstrap?
correct: Resample with replacement and recompute the statistic each time.
Treat the empirical distribution as the population.

distractors.text: Draw new samples from a fitted normal distribution.
Resample without replacement, leaving out one observation at a time.
Split the sample into two halves.
Permute the group labels.
Increase the sample size by repeating the data.

explanation: The bootstrap standard error is the standard deviation of the bootstrap replicates $\hat\theta^*_1,\dots,\hat\theta^*_B$.

stem: How is a percentile bootstrap confidence interval formed?
correct: The $\alpha/2$ and $1-\alpha/2$ quantiles of the replicates.
The middle $1-\alpha$ of sorted estimates.

distractors.text: Add and subtract $1.96$ standard errors from the estimate.
Use the extreme minimum and maximum of the replicates.
Take the quantiles of the original data.
distractors.misconception: uses the sample, not the replicates

distractors.text: Use the standard error from the formula for the mean.
Take the mean of the replicates plus and minus one.

explanation: The percentile interval is transformation-respecting; BCa refines it by correcting for bias and skewness.

stem: How does the jackknife estimate the bias of a statistic $\hat\theta$?
correct: $(n-1)(\bar\theta_{(\cdot)}-\hat\theta)$, from leave-one-out estimates.
Compare the full estimate with leave-one-out averages.

distractors.text: $\bar\theta_{(\cdot)}-\hat\theta$, without the factor $n-1$.
As the standard deviation of the leave-one-out estimates.
As the difference between the mean and the median of the data.
By resampling with replacement many times.
It cannot estimate bias.

explanation: The jackknife-corrected estimate is $n\hat\theta-(n-1)\bar\theta_{(\cdot)}$, which removes the $O(1/n)$ bias.

stem: Where does the jackknife fail?
correct: For non-smooth statistics such as the median.
Sample quantiles are not smooth functions.

distractors.text: For the sample mean.
distractors.misconception: the jackknife works well for the mean

distractors.text: For linear statistics.
distractors.misconception: the jackknife works well for smooth statistics

distractors.text: For any statistic when the sample size is above 100.
For smooth functions of means.
Whenever the data are normal.

explanation: Bootstrap works for the median; neither works for the sample maximum.

stem: In a sample of size $n$, what is the probability that a given observation does not appear in a bootstrap resample?
correct: $(1-1/n)^n$, about $e^{-1}\approx0.368$ for large $n$, so roughly a third is left out.
Each draw misses it with probability $1-1/n$.

distractors.text: $1/n$, the chance that one particular draw picks it.
distractors.misconception: gives the probability of a single draw

distractors.text: One half, since each observation is equally likely to be in or out.
$1-1/n^2$, because pairs of draws are independent.
Exactly zero, since resampling uses all the data.
$(1/n)^n$, the chance of drawing it every time.
distractors.misconception: gives the probability of drawing it every time

explanation: The remaining 63% of observations appear at least once; this is why out-of-bag error is based on roughly a third of the trees in bagging.

stem: How does a kernel density estimator with kernel $K$ and bandwidth $h$ work?
correct: $\hat f(x)=\frac1{nh}\sum_iK\{(x-X_i)/h\}$, a smooth bump averaged over the observations.
Average kernel functions centred at the data.

distractors.text: $\hat f(x)$ is the fraction of data in a fixed bin around $x$.
$\hat f(x)$ is the sample mean of the kernel values at the grid.
It fits a normal density by maximum likelihood.
The kernel is placed at the grid points rather than at the data.
The sum of the bumps is divided by $n$, but not by $h$.
distractors.misconception: omits $1/h$ and does not integrate to one

explanation: The factor $1/h$ keeps the area at 1, since $\int K\{(x-X_i)/h\}dx=h$.

stem: What is the effect of the bandwidth $h$ on a kernel density estimate?
correct: Small $h$ is wiggly and noisy; large $h$ oversmooths and adds bias.
It sets the bias-variance trade-off.

distractors.text: A small $h$ gives a smooth estimate with large bias.
The bandwidth does not affect the shape.
A large $h$ gives a more detailed estimate.
The choice of $h$ matters less than the kernel.
Larger $h$ lowers both bias and variance.

explanation: $\text{bias}\approx h^2f''(x)\mu_2(K)/2$ and $\text{variance}\approx f(x)R(K)/(nh)$; both are balanced by $h\propto n^{-1/5}$.

stem: How does the asymptotically optimal bandwidth (for mean integrated squared error) scale with the sample size $n$?
correct: In proportion to $n^{-1/5}$.
Slowly with $n$.

distractors.text: In proportion to $n^{-1/2}$.
In proportion to $n^{-1}$.
It does not depend on $n$.
In proportion to $n^{1/5}$.
distractors.misconception: has the wrong sign of the exponent

distractors.text: In proportion to $\log n$.

explanation: Parametric densities converge at rate $n^{-1}$ in MISE; this slower rate is the price of flexibility. Silverman's rule is $h=1.06\,\hat\sigma n^{-1/5}$.

stem: Which is true of the choice of kernel in density estimation?
correct: It matters little next to the bandwidth.
Epanechnikov is optimal but others lose little.

distractors.text: The kernel matters more than the bandwidth.
Only the Gaussian kernel gives a valid estimate.
The kernel must be uniform.
A kernel that is not symmetric is optimal.
A kernel with a heavy tail removes bias.

explanation: Kernels are nonnegative, symmetric and integrate to one; they differ in efficiency by under 5%.

stem: What is a known weakness of the kernel density estimator near the boundary of a bounded support?
correct: It leaks mass outside the support and is biased near the edge.
Bumps spill over the boundary.

distractors.text: It is exactly right at the boundary.
It overestimates the density everywhere.
Boundary problems arise only for the Gaussian kernel.
There is no bias but a larger variance.
It cannot be computed at the boundary.

explanation: Examples: densities of returns' absolute values or durations, supported on $[0,\infty)$. Reflecting the data or using log transformations helps.

stem: What does the Nadaraya-Watson estimator of the regression function compute at $x$?
correct: A kernel-weighted average of the responses.
A local mean weighted towards nearby points.

distractors.text: A local linear fit to the nearest points.
The global mean of all responses.
A polynomial fitted to all the data.
The response of the single nearest neighbour.
The slope of a line through the data.

explanation: It is a locally constant fit; as $h\to\infty$ it tends to the sample mean, and as $h\to0$ it interpolates the data.

stem: Why is local linear regression often preferred to Nadaraya-Watson?
correct: Less bias at boundaries, as it fits a line.
Local slope removes edge bias.

distractors.text: It is always faster to compute.
It does not need a bandwidth.
It has no variance.
It fits the global mean.
It applies only to equally spaced data.

explanation: Local linear regression reproduces linear functions exactly, so its bias depends on the curvature only, not on the design density.

stem: What is LOESS (LOWESS)?
correct: Local regression with weights falling with distance.
Weighted local lines.

distractors.text: A global polynomial fit.
A kernel density estimator.
A method for testing normality.
Regression through the origin.
A moving average with equal weights.

explanation: The span (the fraction of points used) plays the role of the bandwidth; a larger span gives a smoother curve.

stem: How is the bandwidth of a kernel regression typically chosen?
correct: By cross-validation, minimising leave-one-out prediction error.
Held-out prediction error.

distractors.text: By taking the smallest value that gives an interpolating fit.
By choosing the largest bandwidth so that the curve is a line.
It is determined by the kernel.
By minimising the in-sample error.
It is fixed at 1 for standardised data.

explanation: The in-sample squared error decreases as $h\to0$, so a held-out criterion (leave-one-out CV, GCV) is needed.

stem: How do nonparametric regression estimators behave as the number of predictors grows?
correct: They suffer the curse of dimensionality: neighbourhoods empty out.
The rate deteriorates with $d$.

distractors.text: They improve with more predictors.
They are unaffected by dimension.
They converge faster than parametric models.
Only the bandwidth changes, not the rate.
The problem arises only in classification.

explanation: Additive or single-index models restore reasonable rates by imposing structure.

stem: Which statement correctly contrasts the Kendall and Spearman distances between two rankings of $n$ items?
correct: Kendall counts discordant pairs of items; Spearman sums squared rank differences.
Kendall is the number of adjacent swaps between the rankings; Spearman squares rank displacements.

distractors.text: Kendall counts the positions where the rankings differ, while Spearman counts the discordant pairs.
distractors.misconception: mixes up the definitions with a position-wise count

distractors.text: Kendall sums squared rank differences, whereas Spearman counts the discordant pairs of items.
Both are at most $n$, because each item can move at most $n$ places in a ranking.
Kendall's distance can be negative, which then signals that the rankings are reversed.
distractors.misconception: confuses a distance with a correlation

distractors.text: Both vanish when one ranking is the exact reverse of the other ranking.

explanation: Both are zero only for identical rankings. The reversed ranking is at the maximum Kendall distance $n(n-1)/2$.

stem: In the Mallows model $P(\pi)\propto\exp\{-\theta\,d(\pi,\pi_0)\}$ with $\theta>0$ and $d$ the Kendall distance, which statement is true?
correct: The centre $\pi_0$ is the mode, and $\theta\to0$ gives the uniform law.
Probabilities fall geometrically with the distance from $\pi_0$, and $\theta=0$ makes all rankings equally likely.

distractors.text: The central ranking is the least likely, since the distance in the exponent is largest there.
distractors.misconception: reverses the sign of the exponent

distractors.text: Probabilities decrease linearly in the distance from the central ranking.
distractors.misconception: confuses geometric decay with linear decay

distractors.text: Letting $\theta\to\infty$ makes all $n!$ rankings equally likely in the limit.
The model needs a separate parameter for every pair of items in the list.
distractors.misconception: confuses it with a saturated pairwise model

distractors.text: Two rankings at the same distance from $\pi_0$ can have different probabilities, depending on which items differ.
distractors.misconception: ignores that only the distance matters

explanation: The probability depends on $\pi$ only through $d(\pi,\pi_0)$, so rankings at equal distance are equally likely. The model has the centre and one concentration parameter.

stem: In a Plackett-Luce model with positive weights $w_1,\dots,w_n$, what is the probability of the ranking $\pi=(\pi_1,\dots,\pi_n)$, listed best first?
correct: $\prod_{i=1}^{n}w_{\pi_i}/\sum_{j\ge i}w_{\pi_j}$.
Each place goes to an unranked item with probability proportional to its weight, and the factors multiply.

distractors.text: $\prod_i w_{\pi_i}/\sum_{j=1}^{n}w_j$, always dividing by the total weight of all items.
distractors.misconception: forgets to remove the items already ranked

distractors.text: $\prod_{i<j}w_{\pi_i}/(w_{\pi_i}+w_{\pi_j})$, a product over all pairs of positions.
distractors.misconception: multiplies pairwise Bradley-Terry probabilities as if independent

distractors.text: $\frac1{n!}\prod_i w_{\pi_i}$, so that every ranking is close to uniform.
distractors.misconception: confuses weights with a uniform prior over rankings

distractors.text: $w_{\pi_1}/\sum_j w_j$, because the first place alone decides the whole ranking.
distractors.misconception: ignores all places after the first

distractors.text: $\sum_i w_{\pi_i}\,(n-i)$, a weighted score of the ranking, as in a Borda count.
distractors.misconception: confuses the probability with a Borda-type score

explanation: With weights $3,2,1$ the ranking $(1,2,3)$ has probability $\frac36\cdot\frac23\cdot1=\frac13$. The factors are renormalised over the remaining items at each place.

stem: How does the Plackett-Luce model relate to Thurstone's model of latent utilities?
correct: Plackett-Luce is the Thurstone model with iid Gumbel errors, taking $w_i=e^{\mu_i}$.
Sorting utilities $\mu_i+\varepsilon_i$ with iid Gumbel noise gives Plackett-Luce rankings.

distractors.text: Plackett-Luce is Thurstone with normal noise and weights $\mu_i$.
They are unrelated, as Thurstone's model is a distance model around a centre.
distractors.misconception: confuses it with the Mallows model

distractors.text: Thurstone models are Plackett-Luce models with all weights equal.
distractors.misconception: thinks the latent scores carry no item effect

distractors.text: Every Thurstone model has the same ranking probabilities as Plackett-Luce.
distractors.misconception: ignores that the noise law decides the model

distractors.text: Thurstone models rank only the top item, while Plackett-Luce ranks the full list.
distractors.misconception: thinks Thurstone gives only a best-choice model

explanation: Thurstone uses latent utilities with noise and ranks by realised value. With normal noise the probabilities have no closed form; with Gumbel noise they reduce to the Plackett-Luce product.

stem: Several judges each rank the same $m$ items. How do the Borda count and the Kemeny consensus ranking compare?
correct: Borda sorts by total points; Kemeny minimises total Kendall distance; they can differ.
Kemeny has the fewest pairwise disagreements with the judges in total, unlike Borda.

distractors.text: Borda and Kemeny always return the same ranking, since both use the judges' full rankings.
Kemeny sorts items by mean rank, whereas Borda minimises the total Kendall distance.
Borda counts only each judge's first choice and ignores the rest of the lists.
The Kemeny ranking is always found at once by sorting the Borda scores of the items.
distractors.misconception: overlooks that Kemeny aggregation is computationally hard

distractors.text: An item preferred to every other item by a majority of judges always has the top Borda score.
distractors.misconception: believes Borda always elects a Condorcet winner

explanation: Borda is a score rule; Kemeny is the median ranking under Kendall distance and is hard to compute in general. With a Condorcet winner Kemeny puts it first, but Borda may not.
